metadata.title: Acute Decompensated Heart Failure with Cardiogenic Shock.

clinicalData.historyPhysical:
History of Present Illness

68-year-old male with history of CAD, previous MI (3 years ago), HTN, and T2DM presents to ED via EMS with acute onset dyspnea and chest pressure that began 4 hours ago. Patient reports progressive orthopnea over past week, now sleeping upright in recliner. Gained 12 pounds in 10 days. Denies chest pain but describes 'heavy pressure.' Reports medication non-adherence due to cost—has not taken furosemide for 2 weeks.

Past Medical History

  • CAD with anterior MI (2023), PCI with stent placement
  • Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), last EF 30%
  • Hypertension
  • Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
  • Chronic kidney disease, Stage 3

Home Medications

  • Furosemide 40 mg daily (not taken × 2 weeks)
  • Carvedilol 12.5 mg BID
  • Lisinopril 20 mg daily
  • Atorvastatin 80 mg daily
  • Metformin 1000 mg BID

Physical Examination

General: Anxious, tripod position, labored breathing

Respiratory: Crackles bilateral bases to mid-lung fields, no wheezing

Cardiovascular: S3 gallop present, JVD to angle of jaw, 3+ pitting edema bilateral lower extremities to knees

Skin: Cool, pale, diaphoretic

Abdomen: Soft, hepatomegaly, positive hepatojugular reflux

.

nursesNotes.author: ED Nurse.
nursesNotes.note: Patient arrived via EMS in acute respiratory distress. Placed on cardiac monitor showing atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. IV access established × 2 (18g bilateral AC). O₂ via NC applied, titrated to 6L for SpO₂ 90%. Patient extremely anxious, stating 'I feel like I'm drowning.' Sitting upright, using accessory muscles. Pink frothy sputum noted when coughing. Skin cool and clammy. Foley catheter inserted—50 mL concentrated, dark amber urine obtained. MD notified. Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg SL given × 1 for chest pressure with minimal relief. Awaiting stat labs and CXR.

nursesNotes.author: ED Nurse.
nursesNotes.note: Patient increasingly lethargic despite continued dyspnea. Urine output 30 mL over past hour (dark, concentrated). BP trending down despite 500 mL NS bolus. Extremities remain cool with delayed cap refill (4 seconds). Patient's daughter at bedside, states father 'doesn't look right—his color is gray.' Lactate 3.2 mmol/L (critical called from lab). BNP >5000 pg/mL. CXR shows bilateral pulmonary edema, cardiomegaly. Cardiology consulted. Patient needs higher level of care. Preparing for MICU transfer. BiPAP setup requested.

nursesNotes.author: MICU Nurse.
nursesNotes.note: Patient transferred to MICU on BiPAP. Tolerating non-invasive ventilation well. Work of breathing decreased, less accessory muscle use. Dobutamine infusion initiated at 5 mcg/kg/min per cardiology. Furosemide 80 mg IV given—good diuretic response with 400 mL clear yellow urine output in first 30 minutes. Skin warmer, color improving from gray to pale pink. Patient more alert, nods appropriately to questions. Daughter reassured. Continuous cardiac monitoring shows conversion to normal sinus rhythm. Will continue to monitor MAP, urine output, and respiratory status closely.

orders.drug: O₂ via nasal cannula, titrate to SpO₂ ≥92%.

radiology.findings: Bilateral pulmonary edema with bat-wing pattern. Cardiomegaly. Small bilateral pleural effusions. No pneumothorax.

ekg.result: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response (rate 118). Old anterior Q waves. No acute ST-segment changes.

echocardiogram.result: Severely reduced LV systolic function, EF 25%. Global hypokinesis with akinetic anterior wall. Moderate mitral regurgitation. Dilated left atrium.

rationale.coreConcept: Cardiogenic Shock in Acute Decompensated Heart Failure.
rationale.caseSummary: Robert Chen represents a classic scenario of preventable ADHF progression triggered by medication non-adherence. After discontinuing furosemide for 2 weeks, he developed progressive volume overload that precipitated acute pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock, marked by hypotension, end-organ hypoperfusion, and elevated lactate.
rationale.answerAnalysis: See option review for detailed analysis.
rationale.goldenRule: In cardiogenic shock, the heart is both the problem and the victim—you cannot improve perfusion with volume alone because the pump cannot handle the load. Inotropic support is mandatory to break the vicious cycle of poor contractility → low output → hypoperfusion → further myocardial dysfunction.

mnemonic.title: PUMP-FAIL
mnemonic.content: P: Perfusion markers; U: Upright positioning; M: MAP goal ≥65; P: Positive-pressure (BiPAP); F: Furosemide (with inotropes); A: Avoid fluids; I: Inotropic support; L: Lactate clearance.
mnemonic.explanation: Reminds clinicians to support the pump while avoiding common pitfalls like excessive fluid or supine positioning.

cheatSheet.title: SHOCK-HF Protocol.
points: Recognize Triad: Hypotension, organ hypoperfusion (cool skin, oliguria, confusion), and elevated lactate.
Immediate Positioning: High-Fowler's to reduce preload.
Early BiPAP: Reduces cardiac workload and improves gas exchange.
Inotropic Support: Mandatory for pump failure (Dobutamine/Milrinone).
Monitor Perfusion: Lactate clearance and MAP are the gold standards.

screens.prompt: The nurse is reviewing the patient's clinical data at 0900 in the ED. Highlight the findings below that require immediate follow-up.
screens.text: The 68-year-old patient presents with acute dyspnea and chest pressure that began 4 hours ago. Vital signs show BP 88/54 mmHg, heart rate 124 bpm irregular, and respiratory rate 28 breaths/min. The patient appears increasingly lethargic despite oxygen support. Physical exam reveals cool, clammy extremities with delayed capillary refill of 4 seconds. Recent labs show lactate 3.2 mmol/L and BNP >5000 pg/mL. The patient has produced only 30 mL of dark, concentrated urine in the past hour.

h1.whyIncorrect: [Hook] While dyspnea and chest pressure are concerning symptoms, they confirm the diagnosis of heart failure rather than indicating shock severity. [Breakdown] The expected symptoms are already captured by the chief complaint—what we need to recognize NOW is the evidence of end-organ damage. [Trap] Don't confuse diagnostic symptoms with shock markers.

h2.whyCorrect: [Hook] BP 88/54 (MAP ~65) represents critical hypoperfusion territory. [Breakdown] This is below the threshold for adequate organ perfusion and meets the hemodynamic criteria for cardiogenic shock. [Trap] A 'normal' systolic of 90 in a hypertensive patient is actually severely low for them.

h3.whyIncorrect: [Hook] Tachycardia is a compensatory response, not a primary shock indicator. [Breakdown] The heart is racing to maintain cardiac output—this is expected physiology, not the problem itself. [Trap] Don't prioritize the body's compensation over the root issue.

h4.whyIncorrect: [Hook] RR 28 is elevated but has improved from admission (was 32). [Breakdown] Respiratory distress is being addressed with O2 support—it's a symptom we're managing, not an unrecognized emergency. [Trap] Trending data matters; this is improving.

h5.whyCorrect: [Hook] Increasing lethargy signals cerebral hypoperfusion—the brain is not getting enough blood. [Breakdown] This is one of the most critical signs of shock because it represents end-organ dysfunction at the highest level. [Trap] Don't dismiss 'tired' as expected; new confusion/lethargy in shock is an emergency.

h6.whyCorrect: [Hook] Cool, clammy skin with 4-second cap refill = peripheral shutdown. [Breakdown] The body is shunting blood away from the extremities to preserve core organs—this is classic shock physiology. [Trap] Warm skin in early septic shock is different; cardiogenic shock = COLD extremities.

h7.whyCorrect: [Hook] Lactate 3.2 mmol/L is above critical threshold (>2.0). [Breakdown] Elevated lactate proves cells are switching to anaerobic metabolism due to inadequate oxygen delivery—this is biochemical evidence of shock. [Trap] Even 'mildly' elevated lactate in the right context is a red flag.

h8.whyIncorrect: [Hook] BNP confirms heart failure but doesn't change immediate management. [Breakdown] We already know he has heart failure—the BNP is diagnostic, not a monitoring tool for acute shock. [Trap] Don't treat the number; treat the patient's perfusion status.

h9.whyCorrect: [Hook] 30 mL/hr of dark urine = renal hypoperfusion. [Breakdown] The kidneys are failing to filter because they're not receiving adequate blood flow—this is a hallmark sign of shock affecting a vulnerable organ. [Trap] Don't normalize low urine output; in shock, kidneys are 'first to fail.'

rationale.answerAnalysis: The correct highlights represent the classic triad of cardiogenic shock: hypotension (h2), altered mental status (h5), peripheral hypoperfusion (h6), elevated lactate (h7), and oliguria (h9). Findings like BNP or dyspnea confirm the underlying diagnosis but are not as critically time-sensitive as the shock indicators.
rationale.clinicalStrategy: Focus on the 'Perfusion Triangle': Pressure (MAP), Periphery (skin/urine), and Products (lactate).

screens.prompt: For each assessment finding below, indicate whether it reflects an expected response to initial heart failure therapy OR indicates worsening cardiogenic shock requiring escalation of care.

rows.text: Increased urine output from 30 mL/hr to 400 mL in 30 minutes after IV furosemide.
rows.rationale: Brisk diuresis after IV furosemide is the desired therapeutic effect.

rows.text: Blood pressure decreased from 92/58 to 88/54 mmHg despite interventions.
rows.rationale: Persistent hypotension despite diuretics indicates the need for inotropic support.

rows.text: Heart rate decreased from 124 bpm irregular to 96 bpm regular on monitor.
rows.rationale: Normalization of rate and rhythm indicates improved cardiac stability.

rows.text: Mental status change from alert/anxious to increasingly lethargic.
rows.rationale: Progressive lethargy indicates worsening cerebral hypoperfusion.

rows.text: Lactate level decreased from 3.2 mmol/L to 1.8 mmol/L.
rows.rationale: Lactate clearance demonstrates improved tissue oxygen delivery.

rationale.coreConcept: Distinguishing therapy success from clinical deterioration.
rationale.answerAnalysis: Improvement in perfusion (lactate, UOP, mentation, rhythm) signals success, while declining MAP or awareness despite standard HF care indicates shock progression requiring inotropes.
rationale.clinicalStrategy: Trend markers: Pressure, Lactate, UOP, and Mentation. Escalation is needed when volume removal alone fails to restore perfusion.

screens.prompt: Based on the patient's current clinical presentation at 0920, which condition represents the highest priority nursing concern requiring immediate intervention?

options.text: Acute anxiety related to dyspnea and fear of suffocation.
options.rationale: Anxiety is a symptom of hypoperfusion, not the root cause. Perfusion must be fixed first.

options.text: Cardiogenic shock secondary to acute decompensated heart failure.
options.rationale: Shock involves global tissue hypoxia and is the top life threat according to ABC priority.

options.text: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response.
options.rationale: AFib with RVR decreases output but is secondary to the primary pump failure (shock).

options.text: Fluid volume overload secondary to medication non-adherence.
options.rationale: Volume overload is the precipitant, but the current acute crisis is shock physiology.

rationale.answerAnalysis: Cardiogenic shock (Option B) is the immediate life threat. Anxiety, AFib, and Volume overload are all relevant but secondary to the circulation (C) failure defined by shock physiology.
rationale.clinicalStrategy: Use the 'Will This Kill My Patient First?' rule. Shock is the most proximal threat to life.

screens.prompt: Complete the diagram below by selecting the priority condition at the center, two nursing actions that address this condition (left side), and two parameters for evaluating treatment effectiveness (right side).

conditions.text: Cardiogenic shock from acute decompensated heart failure.
conditions.rationale: The patient meets all criteria for cardiogenic shock: hypotension, hypoperfusion signs, and elevated lactate in the setting of known HFrEF.

conditions.text: Acute respiratory failure from pulmonary edema.
conditions.rationale: While pulmonary edema is present, it's a consequence of the failing pump—the primary issue is cardiogenic shock.

conditions.text: Medication non-adherence causing heart failure exacerbation.
conditions.rationale: Non-adherence is the root cause but not the immediate priority—we must stabilize the shock first.
Volume overload triggered this episode, but the urgent problem is pump failure causing shock.

actions.rationale: Inotropes improve cardiac contractility and output—mandatory for pump failure.

actions.text: Apply BiPAP to reduce work of breathing and improve oxygenation.
actions.rationale: BiPAP reduces preload/afterload and improves gas exchange without the risks of intubation.

actions.text: Administer additional IV fluid bolus to improve blood pressure.
actions.rationale: Fluids are contraindicated in cardiogenic shock—the heart cannot handle additional volume.

actions.text: Encourage deep breathing and coughing exercises.
actions.rationale: Not appropriate for a patient in acute respiratory distress and shock.

actions.text: Position patient supine to improve venous return.
actions.rationale: Supine positioning would worsen pulmonary edema by increasing venous return.

actions.text: Administer beta blocker to control heart rate.
actions.rationale: Beta blockers are negative inotropes—contraindicated in acute decompensated HF with shock.

parameters.text: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) trending toward ≥65 mmHg.
parameters.rationale: MAP ≥65 is the gold standard perfusion target in shock management.

parameters.text: Serum lactate clearance (decreasing toward normal <2.0 mmol/L).
parameters.rationale: Lactate clearance indicates cells are returning to aerobic metabolism—shock is resolving.

parameters.text: BNP level returning to normal range.
parameters.rationale: BNP changes too slowly (days) to be useful for acute monitoring.

parameters.text: Chest X-ray showing complete resolution of pulmonary edema.
parameters.rationale: CXR changes lag behind clinical improvement—not useful for real-time monitoring.
Anxiety is subjective and secondary to physiological stabilization.
Heart rate normalization is helpful but secondary to perfusion markers.

rationale.answerAnalysis: Inotropes fix the pump; BiPAP reduces workload. MAP and Lactate clearance are the primary objective monitors for shock resolution.
rationale.clinicalStrategy: Fix the Pump (contractility) and the Puddle (pulmonary edema). Monitor objective perfusion markers.

screens.prompt: The nurse is preparing the patient for transfer to the MICU and initiation of BiPAP. Complete the sentence below by selecting the most appropriate action for each dropdown.
screens.text: The nurse should position the patient in %{d1}% and ensure %{d2}% is immediately available at the bedside.

options.rationale: Correct. Upright positioning reduces venous return (preload), decreases pulmonary congestion, and improves diaphragmatic excursion—essential for a patient in pulmonary edema.
Incorrect. Elevating legs increases venous return, which would worsen pulmonary edema in a patient already fluid-overloaded.
Incorrect. While used in some cardiac scenarios, this position does not reduce preload or optimize BiPAP effectiveness for pulmonary edema.
Incorrect. Trendelenburg dramatically increases venous return and would acutely worsen pulmonary edema—this is contraindicated in cardiogenic shock.

options.text: A bag-valve-mask with endotracheal intubation equipment.
options.rationale: Correct. BiPAP can fail in unstable patients; having airway rescue equipment immediately available is a critical safety measure for non-invasive ventilation.
Incorrect. This patient is already fluid-overloaded; additional fluids would worsen pulmonary edema and are contraindicated in cardiogenic shock.
Incorrect. While comfort is important, a commode is not an immediate priority for a patient in respiratory distress requiring BiPAP.

options.text: Beta blocker medication for rate control.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Beta blockers are negative inotropes and are contraindicated in acute decompensated heart failure with cardiogenic shock—they would worsen cardiac output.

dropdowns.correctAnswer: A bag-valve-mask with endotracheal intubation equipment.

rationale.coreConcept: Safety and stabilization during high-risk interventions.
rationale.answerAnalysis: High-Fowler's reduces preload and improves lung mechanics. Airway equipment must be ready because non-invasive ventilation can fail in shock patients.
rationale.clinicalStrategy: Always have a 'Plan B'. Airway rescue is mandatory for unstable BiPAP patients.

screens.prompt: Two hours after transfer to the MICU and initiation of BiPAP with dobutamine infusion, which assessment findings indicate that treatment has been effective? Select all that apply.

options.text: Blood pressure increased from 88/54 to 102/66 mmHg (MAP 65→78 mmHg).
options.rationale: MAP ≥65 mmHg ensures adequate vital organ perfusion pressure—this is the primary hemodynamic goal in shock.

options.text: Heart rhythm converted from atrial fibrillation to normal sinus rhythm.
options.rationale: Rhythm conversion indicates decreased sympathetic stress and better cardiac efficiency with restored atrial kick.

options.text: Urine output increased from 30 mL/hr to 200 mL/hr, urine color light yellow.
options.rationale: Robust diuresis indicates successful renal perfusion and effective fluid mobilization from lungs.

options.text: Respiratory rate decreased from 28 to 18 breaths/min with less accessory muscle use.
options.rationale: Reduced respiratory distress shows BiPAP and inotropes are successfully clearing pulmonary edema.

options.text: Lactate decreased from 3.2 mmol/L to 1.8 mmol/L.
options.rationale: Lactate clearance is the gold standard marker for resolution of cellular hypoxia and successful shock reversal.

options.text: BNP decreased from 5,240 pg/mL to 3,800 pg/mL.
options.rationale: BNP is a diagnostic marker, not an acute monitoring tool—it changes too slowly (days) to reflect short-term treatment response.

rationale.answerAnalysis: Successful shock reversal is marked by improved MAP, lactate clearance, robust diuresis, and reduced respiratory distress. BNP (Option F) is not a reliable marker for acute evaluation.
rationale.clinicalStrategy: Use the 'Rule of Threes': Hemodynamics, Perfusion markers, and Respiratory status must all show improvement.

optionReviews.whyCorrect: MAP ≥65 ensures adequate vital organ perfusion pressure.
Rhythm conversion indicates decreased sympathetic stress and better cardiac efficiency.
Diuresis indicates successful renal perfusion and fluid mobilization.
Reduced respiratory distress shows BiPAP/Inotropes are clearing pulmonary edema.
Lactate clearance is the gold standard for resolution of cellular hypoxia.

optionReviews.whyIncorrect: BNP is a diagnostic marker, not an acute monitoring tool; it changes too slowly.
